digest.intro: AI cold war goes personal, consciousness flickers, and noise becomes signal.

items.title: Jensen Huang's Affair Is Now a National Security File
items.blurb: Huang has admitted the affair in an internal memo after the FT reported that US intelligence believes his partner — an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer — was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation, making this simultaneously a corporate governance crisis, an AI supply-chain security story, and a textbook MSS honeytrap operation at the exact chokepoint of the global chip stack.

items.title: The Pentagon Wants Satellites Around the Moon
items.blurb: Space Force has issued a Request for Information on a 'proliferated cislunar constellation' — an unspecified number of satellites doing undisclosed things near the Moon, following a Trump executive order extending US warfighting doctrine to cislunar space. The Space Force's acquisitions chief is now publicly calling the Moon's orbital vicinity a warfighting domain, which means the geopolitics of orbit have extended roughly 240,000 miles further than last decade.

items.title: Democrats Win the Midterms — Golden Dome Loses Its Shine
items.blurb: Two of Golden Dome's key congressional champions are among the Republicans leaving in the Democratic takeover, and the program — which Trump announced one week into his second term and which has faced essentially zero serious budget scrutiny since — is now heading into hostile appropriations territory. The military had already been quietly backpedaling from the boost-phase intercept capability Trump specifically requested, so the new Congress is walking into a program that was already quietly shrinking.

items.title: Your Brain Flickers Between Two Realities 15 Times a Second
items.blurb: Using Neuropixels probes during binocular rivalry — where each eye sees a different image — Janis Hesse and Doris Tsao found that neurons alternate roughly 15 times per second between representing what you consciously see and what your brain is actively suppressing from awareness. The implication is that consciousness isn't a place in the brain but a timing phenomenon: awareness is what happens when neural firing crosses a temporal threshold, not when it reaches a particular region.

items.title: A Visual Illusion Shows What AI Vision Still Can't Do
items.blurb: The motion aftereffect — stare at a moving thing, then a stationary object appears to drift the opposite direction — turns out to reveal a history-dependent computation in primate IT cortex where objects are encoded in perceptually-shifted coordinates, not just retinal ones. Current AI vision networks simply don't do this: they process each frame statelessly, which is why they're simultaneously superhuman at recognition tasks and blind to exactly the kind of context-dependent, temporally-integrated perception that biological vision runs on.

items.title: A Mitochondrial Protein Nobody Was Watching May Drive Insulin Resistance
items.blurb: Miro1, a GTPase sitting on the outer mitochondrial membrane, accumulates in skeletal muscle in people with Type 2 diabetes — and in preclinical models, removing it restored insulin sensitivity. The kicker: exercise was found to lower Miro1 levels in humans with diabetes, which offers a molecular mechanism for why physical activity improves blood sugar control that's entirely separate from the GLP-1 pathway.

items.title: Physicists Listened to Electrical Noise to Solve a 40-Year Superconductor Mystery
items.blurb: In cuprate superconductors — the materials that superconduct at liquid-nitrogen temperatures and have baffled physicists since the late '80s — a strange state called the pseudogap causes electrons to apparently vanish. Milan Allan's team resolved a decades-long debate about why by measuring Johnson noise, the faint thermal crackle of current, and found that the missing electrons are forming Cooper pairs above the superconducting transition temperature, linking the pseudogap directly to superconductivity rather than treating them as separate phenomena. The elegance is that the 'garbage' signal — noise — was the instrument.

items.title: Stuff Made Here: Engineering a Dog-Mud Solution That Became a Full Mechanical Project
items.blurb: Shane of Stuff Made Here takes a domestic annoyance — dog comes in covered in mud — and treats it as a legitimate engineering problem, which is the whole bit and it never gets old. The channel reliably turns absurd constraints into beautifully over-engineered physical solutions, shot and explained in a way that makes you want to go build something impossible.

facts.fact: The woman US intelligence believes was recruited to spy on Jensen Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was actually a customer of Nvidia — meaning the alleged operation ran through the commercial relationship itself.

Space Force's most distant satellites today are only in geostationary orbit at 22,000 miles — the new cislunar proposal would extend military presence to roughly 240,000 miles, nearly eleven times further.

Neurons in primate visual cortex switch between representing what you consciously see and what your brain is suppressing approximately 15 times per second — roughly the same frame rate as early silent film.

Exercise lowers levels of the protein Miro1 in the skeletal muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes — offering a specific molecular mechanism for a benefit that medicine has observed clinically for decades without fully explaining.

Trump's Golden Dome missile defense program went from announcement to full Pentagon budget commitment with essentially zero serious congressional scrutiny — a fact that is only now becoming a liability as the new Democratic majority takes over appropriations.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film-essay that moves like a consciousness — Tokyo ritual, Guinea-Bissau revolution, Hitchcock, memory, and time, all held together by a system Marker invented from scratch. The form IS the argument. If you haven't seen it, it'll reorganize how you think about images and what they carry.

art_picks.title: Lucas Samaras: Boxes and Reconstructions
art_picks.creator: Lucas Samaras
art_picks.why: Samaras spent decades building obsessive, jewel-encrusted boxes — objects that are simultaneously self-portraits, traps, and altars — and his 1979 Reconstructions fabric paintings, never widely seen, collapse high craft into something hallucinatory. The work sits exactly at the edge of object and body, system and mania.

art_picks.title: Disintegration Loops
art_picks.creator: William Basinski
art_picks.why: Magnetic tape decaying in real time, the signal eating itself — it's a system that runs to its own conclusion and takes beauty with it. Made accidentally during 9/11, the work is about entropy as composition. For someone who thinks in feedback loops and deep time, it hits differently than almost anything.

events.name: Art Week NYC
events.why: New York's first dedicated Art Week pulls over 76 galleries into a coordinated run of openings, artist talks, and walks across the city's major gallery districts — the rare moment the whole scene surfaces at once and the signal-to-noise is actually high.

events.name: Harmony Korine: UX LAM
events.why: Korine's debut with the gallery in New York — his painting practice sits in the same uneasy zone as his films: surface that feels like a glitch, images that shouldn't cohere but do.

events.name: Na Mira: NO SMOKING
events.why: A MoMA opening from an artist working at the intersection of contemporary ritual, image, and system — worth catching in the opening week before the crowds harden.

events.name: John Scofield: Electrospective
events.venue: The Town Hall, 123 W 43rd St, Midtown
events.why: Scofield in a 1,500-seat Midtown theater presenting a career-spanning electric set — jazz guitar that has always been about texture and controlled chaos as much as melody; for someone whose work lives at the edge of digital and physical, there's a formal resonance here.

events.name: artport: A History of Internet Art
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, Meatpacking District
events.why: 25 years of the Whitney's net-art commissioning platform in one show — over 100 works including rebuilt code pieces by Golan Levin and Casey Reas, early-web gate pages treated as the art itself, and a live world premiere of Operator's generative choreography work on Nov 19 & 21-22; the floor plan mimics floating browser windows, which is exactly the kind of formal joke that lands.
